outcome: On 6 Oct 2026 Zhixing You posted arXiv:2610.07537 (single author, revised 7 Oct) claiming a ZFC proof that if κ is strongly compact and GCH holds below κ then GCH holds, which answers Woodin's question affirmatively; I found no independent check, citing paper, or withdrawal as of 13 Oct 2026, and the paper credits GPT-6-Astra and GPT-6.1-Sol with AI assistance in an unspecified role.
problem_asks: Unpacked from the statement alone. (1) Let κ be any strongly compact cardinal; the hypothesis is that GCH holds at every cardinal below κ. (2) The conclusion is that GCH holds 'everywhere', i.e. at every cardinal, including every cardinal at or above κ, which the hypothesis does not cover. (3) The question quantifies over all strongly compact κ: the answer is yes if ZFC proves, for every strongly compact κ, that GCH below κ implies GCH everywhere; it is no if for some strongly compact κ, ZFC plus GCH below κ plus failure of GCH at some cardinal at or above κ is consistent (relative to the large cardinal hypothesis). (4) Setting: the Wikipedia section note says these conjectures concern models of ZFC with choice. The bullet names no object and asks for no bound or constant.

events.what_happened: Zhixing You (Einstein Institute of Mathematics, Hebrew University of Jerusalem; sole author), 'The generalized continuum hypothesis above a strongly compact cardinal', arXiv:2610.07537 [math.LO], 5 pages in v2 (4 pages as listed on the v1 abstract page). Abstract as read in the v1 page (summarised by the fetch tool, not verbatim): 'We answer a long-standing open question of Woodin by proving that if κ is a strongly compact cardinal and GCH holds below κ, then GCH holds.' Theorem A: 'If κ is a strongly compact cardinal and GCH holds below κ, then GCH holds.' Introduction: 'In this paper we answer the question in the affirmative.' The paper states Woodin's question as 'Suppose that κ is strongly compact and GCH holds below κ. Must GCH hold?' and attributes it to Woodin, citing Apter (2000); the introduction also says Woodin asked whether strong compactness alone suffices. Setting: a transitive model V of ZFC with definable elementary embeddings j: V→M; the only large cardinal hypothesis is strong compactness of κ. Per the fetch summary, the argument is an induction on λ ≥ κ assuming 2^{<λ}=λ, using a minimal D ∈ M with j[λ] ⊆ D and |D|^M < j(κ), and a counting lemma (Lemma 3.1) bounding |F ∩ T| by 2^{<λ} for F = {j(A) ∩ D : A ⊆ λ}, giving 2^λ ≤ (2^{<λ})⁺. Remark 3.2 gives a local version for λ-strongly compact κ (2^μ = μ⁺ for infinite μ ≤ λ). Remark 3.3 (in v1, per the fetch) says 'The proofs above don't use crit(j)=κ' and concludes that if κ is ω₁-strongly compact and GCH holds below κ, then GCH holds. The proof details come from a summarising fetch of the arXiv HTML and have not been checked line by line.
events.revisions: v1 submitted 6 Oct 2026 (abstract page lists 4 pages); v2 submitted 7 Oct 2026 (abstract page lists 5 pages). What changed between v1 and v2 is not shown; both HTML versions read through the fetch carry the same acknowledgement sentence and the same Theorem A wording.
events.delivers: In ZFC (V a model of ZFC, with definable class embeddings in the metatheory): for every strongly compact κ, if GCH holds at every cardinal below κ then GCH holds at every cardinal, including those at or above κ. This covers the bullet's full statement as read: hypothesis GCH below κ, conclusion GCH everywhere. The local form (Remark 3.2) gives 2^μ = μ⁺ for μ ≤ λ when κ is λ-strongly compact. Remark 3.3, if correct, extends the conclusion to ω₁-strongly compact κ, a hypothesis weaker than strong compactness; that goes beyond the bullet's hypothesis and is recorded only as a claim.
events.remains: On the paper's own claim, no part of the bullet's statement remains open, provided Theorem A is correct and the conclusion 'GCH holds' is read as GCH at all cardinals (the paper's conclusion is not written as 'everywhere'). Nothing in the record independently confirms that reading or the proof. The ZFC-with-choice setting fixed by the section note is the setting the paper uses, per the fetch summary.
events.time_since_posted: 7 days as of 13 Oct 2026 (v1 posted 6 Oct). No engagement found in the index searched; coverage of the index for the last week is thin, so this is weak evidence of silence.
events.doubts: (a) Single author; the paper is about 4 to 5 pages and claims to settle a question that Apter (2000, cited by the paper), Dimopoulos (arXiv 1710.05743, 2017) and Apter, Dimopoulos and Usuba (arXiv 1901.05313, Jan 2019, Question 5.2) all treat as open. (b) The only statement about AI is an acknowledgement that names two systems and says they were 'invoked dynamically during the investigation'; no sentence says which step, if any, the model supplied, or that a human checked each step. (c) Remark 3.3 claims a strictly larger class of cardinals works because the proof 'doesn't use crit(j)=κ'; this is a strong extension stated in a remark, and I could not check it. (d) No Lean or Coq artefact is mentioned in the paper as read. (e) My account of Lemma 3.1 and the induction comes from a summarising fetch, not from reading the PDF, so a gap in the counting step would not be visible to me. None of these is an identified error.
events.direction: Affirmative: the implication asked about holds for every strongly compact κ, so GCH below κ forces GCH everywhere. The paper says 'we answer the question in the affirmative'. No counterexample or object is involved.

events.what_happened: Gabriel Goldberg, 'Strong Compactness and the Ultrapower Axiom', arXiv:1710.03586 (submitted 10 Oct 2017), an announcement of consequences of an abstract comparison principle. The ar5iv rendering gives Theorem 2 (UA): 'GCH holds above the least strongly compact cardinal', with 2^λ = λ⁺ for every λ ≥ κ when κ is the least strongly compact cardinal. The result is conditional on the Ultrapower Axiom (UA).
events.revisions: Not checked. I read the 2017 abstract page and the ar5iv rendering only. Goldberg's later full paper 'The Ultrapower Axiom and the GCH' (math.berkeley.edu/~goldberg/Papers/UAandGCH.pdf) was not read; the PDF was not fetchable.
events.delivers: Under UA only: GCH above the least strongly compact cardinal, i.e. 2^λ = λ⁺ for all λ ≥ κ, where κ is the least strongly compact. Restricted to the least strongly compact cardinal and to UA; no ZFC claim.
events.remains: The bullet's ZFC question for an arbitrary strongly compact κ, and the GCH-below hypothesis for it. Without UA nothing here follows.
events.direction: Affirmative conditional on UA, for the least strongly compact cardinal only. It does not assume GCH below κ and says nothing about ZFC.

The sentence has no citation of its own; the next sentence contrasts it with 'the one in [3]', which is Goldberg's 'Strongly compact cardinals and the GCH, revisited' (to appear). I could not find that paper.

events.direction: Affirmative conditional on UA, least strongly compact cardinal only; a remark, not a theorem in this paper.

events.what_happened: Arthur W. Apter, 'On some questions concerning strong compactness', Archive for Mathematical Logic 51 (7–8) (2012), 819–829. The PhilPapers and Springer abstract pages were blocked or redirected, so I did not read the abstract verbatim. Secondary summaries of the abstract say it treats Woodin's question and two variants, and that it gives a negative answer and a positive answer for a supercompact κ, both in the absence of the full Axiom of Choice. The summaries disagree on whether the negative answer is to Woodin's question itself or to its first variant.

It extends several results of Apter on symmetric extensions and works in two settings: V a model of ZFC, and V a model of ZF + DC_κ. Its results concern preservation of DC_{<κ}. The abstract page does not state Woodin's question or GCH above a strongly compact cardinal.

events.direction: No bearing on the bullet's answer; out of scope by setting (ZF + DC and symmetric extensions) and by subject (dependent choice).

disputes.summary: Apter (2012), as summarised, gives negative or split answers to Woodin's question and its variants in a setting without full choice; You (2026) gives a positive answer in ZFC. The two are compatible because they work in different settings. The Apter abstract was not read verbatim, so the exact scope of Apter's negative answer is unverified.

summary: The only event that addresses the bullet's ZFC question is arXiv:2610.07537 by Zhixing You, submitted 6 Oct 2026 and revised 7 Oct. Its Theorem A reads 'If κ is a strongly compact cardinal and GCH holds below κ, then GCH holds', and its introduction says 'In this paper we answer the question in the affirmative'. The paper states Woodin's question as 'Suppose that κ is strongly compact and GCH holds below κ. Must GCH hold?', so its hypothesis and conclusion match the bullet; the bullet's 'everywhere' is read as GCH at all cardinals. I read the paper only through two arXiv HTML fetches, each summarised by a fetch model; the PDF returned binary. The quotes (abstract, Theorem A, the question's wording, the acknowledgement) agree across the v1 and v2 readings, but none is checked against the PDF, and my account of the proof (the minimal-D argument, Lemma 3.1's bound |F ∩ T| ≤ 2^{<λ}, the induction giving 2^λ ≤ (2^{<λ})⁺) is a summary of a summary. The acknowledgement reads: 'This work used AI assistance from GPT-6-Astra with the ultra reasoning setting, with GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra invoked dynamically during the investigation.', followed by 'The author takes full responsibility for the paper.' Nothing in the paper says which step, if any, the model produced, whether the proof idea came from it, or whether a human checked the argument. So I record both systems with the authors' sentence and leave the load-bearing call open: on one reading the work is AI-assisted research in which the model's role is unstated; on the other, the disclosure is a generic 'assistance' line. The phrase 'ultra reasoning setting' does not match the reasoning levels I found in third-party documentation of GPT-6 Astra (low through max), so I record the author's wording without reconciling it. As of 13 Oct 2026, seven days after v1, my searches found no reaction, no MathOverflow thread, no blog post, no citing paper and no withdrawal. The search index is thin for the past week, so this silence is weak evidence. Earlier work gives only conditional or different-setting answers. Goldberg's UA results give GCH above the least strongly compact cardinal (arXiv 1710.03586, Oct 2017, Theorem 2 (UA), per the ar5iv rendering) and above a supercompact (arXiv 1810.05036, Oct 2018), and a remark in Goldberg's 'Fréchet cardinals' (arXiv 1810.05035, Section 12) repeats the least-strongly-compact claim under UA; I record these as discounted by scope, since they assume UA or a supercompact. Apter's 2000 paper 'On a problem of Woodin' is the cited origin of the question and I did not read it. Apter (2012) is summarised as giving a negative answer in a setting without full choice, which the section's ZFC-with-choice note excludes. Apter's 2024 JSL paper (GCH failing at every inaccessible except the least measurable κ0, which is strongly compact in the model) is consistent with Theorem A: since κ0 is a limit of inaccessibles, GCH fails below κ0 in that model, so the hypothesis fails; I checked this from the abstract only. Banerjee (2019) is a ZF+DC symmetric-extension result and is out of scope. Apter–Dimopoulos–Usuba (arXiv 1901.05313, Jan 2019, Question 5.2) and Dimopoulos (arXiv 1710.05743, 2017) list the question, or the related forcing question, as open; those are 'still open' statements, not events. The AI search turned up OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra announcement of Aug 2026 (ten claimed results, none in set theory according to SiliconAngle and The Decoder; the OpenAI page itself was blocked), and a report dated 9 Oct 2026 of an OpenAI preprint on the Partition Principle that set theorist Asaf Karagila criticised; that is a different problem and I did not research it. Several unrelated arXiv papers name 'GPT-6 Astra' or 'Astra 6' in their AI disclosures; I saw them only in search snippets.
competing_reading: The case against crediting the result: the only support is a 4-to-5-page single-author preprint, posted a week ago, whose AI role is undisclosed, whose proof I could not read directly, and which claims to settle a question the literature has listed as open since at least 2000. Short proofs of long-open questions with an undisclosed AI role have a high prior of a gap, and Remark 3.3's extension to ω₁-strongly compact cardinals is a stronger claim than the main theorem. The case for reading it as a genuine ZFC answer, once verified: the hypotheses and conclusion match the bullet, the tools named (definable embeddings, a minimal D with |D|^M < j(κ), a cardinal-arithmetic count) are the standard ones for this kind of cardinal-arithmetic bound, and the consistency results I checked (Apter 2024, Goldberg's UA results, Apter 2012 in its no-choice setting) do not contradict it. A reader who takes 'GCH holds' as weaker than GCH at all cardinals would not get the bullet's answer, but I see no textual basis for that reading.
what_would_settle_it: A public verification or refereed acceptance of Theorem A by a set theorist (ideally with a Lean or similar formalisation of the counting lemma); a verbatim check of the abstract, Theorem A, the question statement and the acknowledgement against the PDF; the v1-to-v2 difference; a statement from the author on which step the GPT-6-Astra and GPT-6.1-Sol outputs contributed and what the author checked; a check of Remark 3.3; and any later paper that either builds on the result or still lists the question as open without citing it. For the older events, reading Apter (2000) and the Apter (2012) abstract verbatim would settle whether any no-choice result touches the ZFC question.

The sentence does not say which mathematical step, idea or check the model contributed. The same section says 'The author takes full responsibility for the paper.' 'Ultra reasoning setting' is the author's wording; in third-party documentation of GPT-6 Astra I found reasoning levels low through max and no setting named 'ultra' for it, so I have not reconciled the phrase with an official setting.

events.credibility_reason: A 4-5 page single-author preprint posted seven days ago claims to settle a question listed as open since 2000. Remark 3.3 extends the result to ω₁-strongly compact cardinals, a much stronger claim that the record could not check. The proof was read only through summaries. No error has been identified, and seven days is too short to expect uptake, so this is not not_credible.

judgement.why: You (2026) states Theorem A as exactly the statement: strongly compact κ with GCH below κ implies GCH. So it is scope whole. It has no named reader and was posted a week ago, so it is unreviewed. I marked it doubtful, not not_credible: it is very short, the proof was seen only through summaries, and Remark 3.3's extension to ω₁-strongly compact cardinals is suspiciously strong, but no error is identified and a week is too short to expect any uptake. AI role was the close call. The only evidence is an acknowledgement that the work 'used AI assistance' with the models 'invoked dynamically during the investigation'. It does not say the models produced any argument, construction or case in the result. Under the rule that a thin quote with no stated contribution is none, I answered none. The Goldberg results assume the Ultrapower Axiom (and in one case supercompactness), and Apter (2012) works without full choice, so all are variants. Apter (2000) was never read and Banerjee (2019) is about a different subject, so both are none.
judgement.doubts: The AI role for You (2026) could reasonably be read as assisted: 'invoked dynamically during the investigation' implies the models took part in the research, but the paper never says what they produced. If the author later discloses that a model supplied a step, this should change to assisted or generated. The paper's text, including the acknowledgement, was read only through fetch-tool summaries and not checked against the PDF. Remark 3.3 should be checked by an expert, since a false strong extension would cast doubt on the main argument.
